newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa ends up, July soars to contract high.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa ends up, July soars to contract high.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures closed sharply higher, scoring fresh contract highs amid rising concerns weather patterns may disrupt plantings for the new cocoa crop.

July gapped higher at the outset, leaving a chart gap between Wednesday's high of 1,026 stg per tonne and Thursday's low of 1,036. Buy-stops were triggered, boosting prices past resistance near 1,040 to set-off more buy-stops and attract new long positions.
Analysts said the developing El Nino weather pattern could bring drought to major weather-producing regions and disrupt plantings for the new crop, although it was rather early to make forecasts.

Earlier this week, U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said warm ocean temperatures off the western coast of South America had triggered an El Nino weather pattern, which could bring damaging weather to cocoa-growing areas.
Southeast Asian countries, including thrd-largest producer Indonesia, were already watching for possible drought resulting from El Nino.

"I will be keeping a close eye on production levels in June and July to see if there has been any impact," a senior Indonesian cocoa industry official said on Thursday. "It is already getting difficult to get cocoa beans now."
Further support came from fresh talk that Ivory Coast settings remained low for the next year's crop, traders said.
Once triple July resistances were broken early in the session between 1,040 and 1,060, which pulled July up and out of a flag formation, purchases accelerated as funds joined the buying frenzy.
Total turnover amounted to 30,714 contracts, the highest volume day since March 31, 1995 when turnover was 48,554 lots. September was by far the most popular contract, tallying 13,565 trades.
Front-month July came in third with 5,165, behind March 1998's 6,800. Traders said July turnover was less robuts because the contract was closing in on expiration.
September also grabbed the most interest because more information about mid-crops and weather effects on the new crop would emerge around that time, traders said.
September's action was also reflected in the market's structure. September/December lost 17 stg, with December trading at a 21-stg discount to September. Most other spreads were close to steady.

When New York confirmed cocoa's upmove with a sharply higher open and CSCE July's racing above $1,500 per tonne, July and September here each ran up to fresh contract highs on fresh buying and some arbitrage.
July peaked at its new contract high at 1,088 stg and September at 1,107 before light profit-taking and light origin selling set in to cap gains.
July's previous contract high was 1,085 and September's was 1,096, both set on August 21, 1996.
Despite a close off the session highs, traders were still optimistic on cocoa because of the encouraging fundamentals if weather disrupts settings for the new crop.

Options activity remained subdued despite surging futures. Twenty-five September 1,000-stg puts and 50 September 1,025 puts changed hands. Traders said locals were the main buyers of the 1,025 puts near 24-percent volatility.
